title: Is Expensive Bottled Water Actually Better for You?
gist: The premium bottled water category is built on a mix of real mineral-driven taste differences and marketing associations (purity, alkaline pH, high TDS, remote sourcing) that imply health benefits the evidence does not support. Experts quoted argue luxury water is best understood as a dining or taste category rather than superior hydration, and that glass packaging does not eliminate microplastic exposure.

insights.claim: The premium bottled water industry has converted a commodity into a differentiated category, with supermarket shelves distinguishing glacial, iceberg, volcanic, spring, mineral, and alkaline water, restaurants introducing water menus, and trained water sommeliers assessing bottles on mineral composition, mouthfeel, and provenance.
insights.speaker: Megan Tomos
insights.so_what: Category segmentation and on-premise water menus are the mechanism by which a zero-margin commodity gains pricing power, a template applicable across other undifferentiated consumer staples.
insights.quote: Water is supposed to be the simplest thing we consume. The premium bottled water industry has transformed it into something that requires a backstory.

insights.claim: Consumers treat label terms such as 'rich in minerals', high TDS numbers, and alkaline pH as automatic markers of superior quality, when in reality none of those numbers tell you anything on their own.
insights.speaker: Maria Abi Hanna
insights.so_what: Premium price signaling rests on metrics that carry no standalone meaning, a vulnerability if nutrition-labeling tools and regulators make composition more legible to shoppers.

insights.so_what: TDS is the category's most-cited differentiator yet is not a quality metric, so brands leaning on it are marketing an uninterpretable number.

insights.claim: A 2025 study led by France's Agency for Food, Environmental and Occupational Health and Safety (ANSES) found microplastics in beverages packaged in glass, tracing many particles not to the glass but to the painted coating on metal bottle caps, which could become scratched as caps rubbed together during storage.
insights.speaker: Megan Tomos
insights.so_what: Undercuts the premium glass safety narrative and shifts scrutiny to closures, an overlooked component in packaging supply chains.

insights.claim: In the ANSES results, soft drinks and beer in glass bottles contained considerably more particles than the same drinks in other packaging, while water contained far fewer particles overall, though glass-bottled water averaged slightly more than water packaged in plastic or cartons.
insights.speaker: Megan Tomos
insights.so_what: The counterintuitive finding that glass-bottled water carries slightly more particles than plastic or cartons complicates the premium packaging thesis across the beverage complex, not just water.
insights.locator: The results also varied by beverage.

insights.claim: The ANSES study does not prove glass packaging is more dangerous than plastic; it demonstrates that changing the bottle material does not eliminate every other potential source of plastic exposure.
insights.speaker: Megan Tomos
insights.so_what: Material substitution alone is not a credible contamination fix, so packaging-led premium claims need whole-system validation to hold up.
